sentences.text: This creature featured a long, flattened snout equipped with interlocking teeth resembling those of modern crocodiles.
Its body was protected by robust bony armor that might have been overlaid with soft, leathery tissue.
Researchers estimate the skull measured about 37 centimeters in length, while the lower jaw could extend to 43 centimeters.
Air intake occurred through nostrils positioned at the very front and top of the snout.
The quadratojugal bone was notably small and did not assist in connecting the lower jaw.
The genus was first formally described by Price in 1955.
Llewellyn Ivor Price named the animal based on fossils discovered near Peirópolis.
The initial scientific description relied mainly on parts of the skull.
Specimens of the type species were originally found within the Serra da Galga Formation.
Subsequent discoveries indicate the animal also inhabited the Presidente Prudente Formation.
Scientists interpret this animal as living partly in the water.
The presence of bony plates is cited as proof of this semi-aquatic way of life.
A tail flattened on its sides and ridged armor likely improved swimming efficiency.
Marinho and colleagues suggest these ridges provided stability and streamlined movement when submerged.
In 2004, Carvalho and colleagues created the family Itasuchidae to group Itasuchus with Malawisuchus.
This family was later redefined by Pinheiro and colleagues in 2018 to encompass other similar forms.
It is often believed that Itasuchus and its kin were close relatives of the Peirosauridae within the Notosuchia clade.
The animal lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, spanning between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
It inhabited river systems during the late Campanian and early Maastrichtian stages.
The environment likely featured an arid to semi-arid climate with occasional wetter periods.
It remains debated whether Caririsuchus camposi belongs to Itasuchus, a suggestion by Buffetaut that lacked widespread acceptance.
Some researchers question placing Itasuchus in Trematochampsidae due to potential problems with the holotype of Trematochampsa.
The specific family classification of Itasuchus is also disputed, with Trematochampsidae proposed as an uncertain alternative.
